subtopic: NATO-REPORT BY MINISTER RESPECTING CANADIAN FORCES IN EUROPE UPON RETURN FROM BRUSSELS MEETING

speakeroldname: Hon. Leo Cadieux (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: NATO-REPORT BY MINISTER RESPECTING CANADIAN FORCES IN EUROPE UPON RETURN FROM BRUSSELS MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in keeping with the undertaking I previously gave to the house, I would like at this time to report to honourable members on the meeting in Brussels last Wednesday of the NATO Defence Planning Committee. At the same time, I would like to table copies of the communique in English and French and suggest that they be attached as an annex to today's proceedings.
The first step of the NATO planning cycle is agreement by the Defence Ministers on the guidance to be given to the military authorities, who subsequently expand these guidelines into detailed force plans. This first step is what we were engaged in last Wednesday.
The meeting was of special interest to Canada because it was at this time that we had undertaken to begin discussions on Canadian proposals for changes in the Canadian Forces in Europe.
The communique refers to this in paragraph 5 which reads:
Mr. Cadieux, Canadian Minister of National Defence, explained to the Defence Planning Committee the policy and general intention of his government concerning the Canadian Forces in Europe. The Defence Planning Committee discussed procedures for consultation. The first step will be a discussion of the Canadian proposals between the Canadian and NATO military authorities in the immediate future.

In explaining to the defence planning committee the policy and general intention of the Canadian government concerning the Canadian Forces in Europe, I said that as a consequence of the defence review, the Canadian government had reaffirmed its belief in collective security, and reaffirmed Canada's membership in NATO and the importance of NATO to Canada's security. I said, also, that while Canada planned a phased reduction in the size of its forces in Europe, it would be maintaining a significant military presence there.
I pointed out that the North Atlantic Alliance is not just an alliance for the defence of Europe, but that the North Atlantic area includes North America as well, and defence efforts in North America do contribute to the security of Europe.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
With respect to restructuring of the Canadian Forces, I said our forces in Europe now require different equipment and training from the forces we maintain in Canada for North American defence. We plan to restructure the Canadian Forces over a period of time so that the equipment and training for their roles at home and abroad will be compatible. With the completion of this process, in addition to
June 2, 1969

Canadian Forces in Europe a separate air element Canada will have a modern, mobile but smaller land force stationed in Europe. This represents a precise response to the need for land force elements in NATO with a high degree of readiness, flexibility and mobility.
There has been a good deal of speculation about the forces which we will have in Europe. Since the consultations have just started, and will take some time to complete, it is not possible for me to say what our final posture in Europe will be. The proposals which we have put forward would involve the conversion of the mechanized brigade group to an air-transportable combat group with helicopter support. In addition we proposed that the air element be equipped initially with C.F.-104's.
I took the opportunity while in Brussels to discuss the Canadian proposals informally with defence ministers of Belgium, Germany, The Netherlands, United Kingdom and United States, whose countries have forces stationed in central Europe. I also explained these proposals to the defence ministers of Denmark and Norway. All of the ministers with whom I spoke were very frank in expressing their concern as to the extent of the changes and reductions involved. They sought full consultation in accordance with the agreed NATO procedures.
Canada has always met her obligations fully and will continue to do so. In the North Atlantic Treaty Alliance every member has the right to change its commitments but at the same time has an obligation to follow the procedures of consultation which have been established. These arrangements have been designed in the best interests of NATO and we want to make certain that we have the full benefit of these consultations concerning the changes we are proposing. Therefore I might not be able to report fully on these matters before these consultations have been completed.
These procedures for consultation on changes in national contributions require that discussions take place in the first instance with the NATO military authorities and with the defence planning committee, both in permanent and ministerial sessions. In the normal course of events, as I mentioned in the house on April 24, these consultations are carried out during the annual defence planning review with final undertakings being made on each nation's force contributions for the next year at the regular ministerial meeting of the defence planning committee in December.

It has been, of course, my intention to have adequate consultation with our allies on any changes we make. I assured my NATO colleagues that while we did not propose to reconsider the policy decisions announced on April 3 we would follow the consultation procedure fully both in letter and in spirit. Our proposals have already been placed before the NATO military authorities. I am confident that when the consultations are completed we will come to conclusions that are satisfactory both to Canada and to our allies.
The planning of the future posture of our forces both in Europe and in Canada will be proceeding in parallel with consultations with our NATO allies. Our intention is to achieve the new posture over the next three years. The new posture will avoid very substantial increases in the defence budget which otherwise would have occurred. We believe we can achieve the transition, barring unexpected international developments, within a defence budget which will be maintained for the next three years at its current dollar level.
Hon. members are understandably anxious to obtain detailed information on changes in our armed forces, a matter of vital concern to all Canadians. Mr. Speaker, this anxiety is shared by members of the Canadian Armed Forces themselves and is indeed magnified by their personal involvement. We are determined that changes we make will be in the best interests of Canada, and at the same time we must and do recognize that we have an obligation and a commitment to the members of the forces.
In this regard we intend to be absolutely sure that all decisions are made with consideration being given to how they will affect these loyal and dedicated Canadians to whom we owe so much. I intend to make periodical progress reports as decisions are reached.

subtopic: NATO-REPORT BY MINISTER RESPECTING CANADIAN FORCES IN EUROPE UPON RETURN FROM BRUSSELS MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) has said, "It is not possible for me to say what our final posture in Europe will be". It seems clear that the Minister of National Defence is still trying to borrow time to convince some of his colleagues to be more reasonable in their approach to Canada's responsibilities to our NATO allies.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made a statement on April 3, a so-called declaration of principle, setting out so-called priorities and announcing a "planned and phased reduction" in our military contribution to NATO in Europe. Since that time the Prime
June 2, 1969

Minister made a somewhat notorious speech in Calgary. He has attempted to answer questions about the policy in the House of Commons; the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) and the Minister of National Defence have tried to explain the policy to our allies; the civil servants have tried to understand it, and now the military must try to implement it. The harder they try to explain what the policy is all about, the more they try to justify it, the harder they try to draft a plan to implement it, the clearer it becomes that the original statement of principle was harebrained and irresponsible, and subsequent statements have only made it worse. The Prime Minister made speeches insisting that defence policy must flow from foreign policy. Foreign policy is still under review. But he has already decided to reduce our role in the European alliance and increase it in the North American alliance. On what basis? For what reason? We will not know presumably until the review of foreign policy catches up with what he wants to do in defence policy.
On previous occasions the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has stated the position of our party. First of all we regard this decision as a retreat to isolationism and con-tinentalism. The government intends virtually to withdraw from a wider alliance in Europe to concentrate on the narrower partnership with the United States. This we believe is reactionary and ill-advised.
Second, it is clear that the decision of the government of Canada will hurt the chances to detente in Europe. It seems to be the view of all our NATO partners that any reduction in forces should be made jointly between NATO and the Warsaw pact countries. Cana-ada's unilateral reduction undermines the NATO position and effectively postpones any meaningful negotiations toward detente. It will be difficult or perhaps impossible for NATO to enter negotiations with its hand weakened. Third, the decision of the government, by weakening the conventional strength of NATO, lowers the-so-called-nuclear threshold and increases the likelihood of any conflict escalating into a nuclear exchange very quickly.
Canada is being made to look ridiculous; and Canada's defence policy looks as if it is in the hands of erratic and confused amateurs. Even worse is the fact that there is a fundamental hypocrisy to the position of the Canadian government. The minister returned on April 14 from the spring meeting of NATO 29180-589J

Canadian Forces in Europe ministers in Washington and tabled in this house a copy of the communique issued by the NATO meeting, a communique which the minister agreed to on behalf of the government of Canada and which the government of Canada pretends to support.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
That communique said in part:
The allies participating in the NATO integrated defence program agreed that it was extremely important that during an era of negotiation the defence posture of the alliance should not be relaxed and that premature expectations of solutions to outstanding questions should not be generated. The maintenance of effective defence is a stabilizing factor and a necessary condition for effective detente policies.
The communique then continued:
Accordingly these members of the alliance reaffirmed their continuing determination to make appropriate contributions to joint efforts for defence and deterrents at all levels both nuclear and conventional. They accepted the continuing need for the current NATO strategy based on a forward defence and appropriate response to any aggression, and for a credible conventional and nuclear deterrent including adequate over-all and local force levels. The necessary military posture of the alliance consists of the strategic nuclear deterrent forces, the presence of sufficient substantial and effective North American and European conventional forces as well as supporting tactical nuclear forces in the European area and adequate ready reinforcements.
On May 2, speaking in this house, the minister once again stated his own position on the question of NATO, a position which is so clearly at variance with the position of the Prime Minister. The minister on May 2 stated his agreement with General Lemnitzer's comment to the effect that there should be no over-all military reduction of the NATO capability overseas.
Now we have the minister returning from Brussels, where he attended the meeting of the NATO defence planning committee. While there, the minister supported, on behalf of the government of Canada, a communique which said in part that NATO military capability "should not be reduced, except as part of a pattern of mutual force reductions balanced in scope and timing" with the Warsaw pact countries.
It is perfectly obvious that the Minister of National Defence cannot continue to endorse statements such as those I have read, and continue on the other hand to try to support the policy dictated by the Prime Minister. By pretending to support the purposes and the strategy agreed upon by NATO, the minister does not help improve the credibility of
June 2, 1969

Canadian Forces in Europe Canada, and he is quickly destroying his own credibility with those who serve under him in the armed forces, and with his counterparts and colleagues in the other NATO countries.
As far as defence policy is concerned, if the Prime Minister wants to live a lie he should be left to do so, but I should hope that the Minister of National Defence would not lend himself to what is becoming a two-faced policy which would make Canada an international hypocrite.

subtopic: NATO-REPORT BY MINISTER RESPECTING CANADIAN FORCES IN EUROPE UPON RETURN FROM BRUSSELS MEETING
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: NATO-REPORT BY MINISTER RESPECTING CANADIAN FORCES IN EUROPE UPON RETURN FROM BRUSSELS MEETING
speechtext:
Some of our allies have estimated that the plans of the Canadian government would amount to a 66 per cent reduction in the number of Canadian troops in Europe and an 80 per cent reduction in efficiency. I hope sincerely, as I am sure the majority of Canadian people hope, that this estimate is incorrect.
I want to conclude by saying that we are still hopeful, as are the Canadian people, that this country is being led by a man who understands this nation's obligations to our allies, both contractual and moral, and that those hopes will not be dashed by further policy announcements. The government's policy is wrong in concept; it is inconsistent with the support of NATO obligations and strategy, and it gives Canada a reputation that few Canadians want-that of a country unwilling to pull its weight or do its fair share in collective defence of western civilization.

subtopic: NATO-REPORT BY MINISTER RESPECTING CANADIAN FORCES IN EUROPE UPON RETURN FROM BRUSSELS MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of this party welcome the statement of the Minister of National Defence that the Canadian government intends to carry out a phased reduction of our military commitments in Europe and a change in Canada's military role. This party has for the past five years advocated that there ought to be a phased reduction of our military commitments in Europe and an eventual withdrawal of our military commitments there.
I think it is unfortunate that the minister has not been able to give us more information as to what goal he has in mind and the degree of flexibility both with respect to the size of the forces and the length of time over which this reduction will take place. There have been stories emanating from Brussels that the Canadian force will be reduced by some two-thirds between now and 1972. I do not know whether this was information deliberately leaked to the press as a trial balloon,

or whether the minister has some other figure in mind.
It seems to me that our allies know what the government has in mind, and members of the press seem to be able to get information, but parliament seems always to be the last to know what the government has in mind. We would like to know from the minister, and I hope he will tell us in the course of the next few days, just what the government's goal is with respect to this phased reduction, over what length of time it will take place, and whether the minister himself has altered his objectives during the last few days as a result of his discussion in Brussels.
It is quite apparent that there is a good deal of pressure on the minister and the government to change the policy which they have enunciated. The statements of Defence Secretary Melvin Laird of the United States, Defence Minister Dennis Healey of Great Britain, and others, indicate that there has been criticism and complaint in this respect. I hope the government will make it perfectly clear that this is a matter for Canada to decide and the decision must be made in the light of Canada's best interests, having in mind our interests as a nation and our responsibility to the United Nations and the security of the world.
Something has been said about contractual obligations. I do not need to remind the house that when NATO was formed in 1949 there was no commitment on Canada's part to supply military forces in Europe. That arose on a temporary basis to meet the situation occasioned by the Korean war. We in this party maintain that the situation in Europe has changed, and consequently our policy and temporary commitments are no longer binding upon Canada. I hope therefore that the minister will be firm. We understand of course that there have to be negotiations and consultations with our allies. But I hope there will be no compromise and no weakening of the government's position that Canada proposes to play a different military role and that it proposes to reduce substantially its forces in Europe.
As a matter of fact, we in this party believe that the situation in Europe has altered to the point where we should withdraw our military commitment in Europe. Those who are fearful of the military situation in Europe forget that there is a resurgent Germany, that -the NATO forces now have the advantage of tactical nuclear weapons in the order of 7 to 1 over their opponents, and
June 2, 1969

that the dangers which required the sending of Canadian troops to Europe in 1951, 1952 and 1953 are no longer present.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
I am disappointed that the only statements which have been made by the government with reference to NATO have had to do solely with our military commitments. We have always been told by the government that NATO is more than a military alliance, that it has a political role to play, and that the political role is not only ensuring collective security but extending democracy and working out a system by which the nations of Europe can live together in peace. I submit that we are not very credible when we have a NATO agreement under which the signatories pledge themselves to defend and expand their democratic institutions, while at the same time we have an ally like Greece trampling democracy underfoot in a shameful manner, and Portugal carrying on a colonial war in Angola. We heard nothing from the government in protest about this state of affairs.
We believe that NATO is more than a military alliance. It is also a political vehicle to establish security and peace in Europe. Only a few weeks ago the government of Finland extended an invitation to a European security conference to be held in Helsinki, and to be attended by the NATO nations and the Warsaw pact nations. To date, both our government and the governments of our allies have been callously indifferent to this invitation or have smothered it in moth-eaten excuses. We believe that the government of Canada should be using its membership in NATO in an attempt to break the present Maginot Line complex of two groups of powers glaring at each other over a border. We should be using our influence to follow up every peace feeler that is advanced, in the hope of ending the cold war and establishing a European security pact in Europe. I hope that the government will give as much attention to the question of our political role in NATO as they have been giving to the military role which we perform in that organization.

Mr. Speaker, we listened with great interest to the statement made by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux), and we notice that we are still at the study and assessment stage with regard to Canadian forces in Europe and the Canadian defence policy as a whole.
Canadian Forces in Europe
One point strikes me especially, Mr. Speaker, and I would like to commend the minister for that; it is that national defence has always been in a way a white elephant for Canada from the budgetary as well as the political standpoints, and has always been criticized by the opposition parties as well as by government members, as is evidenced by the dissension within the government.
But it is a fact, Mr. Speaker, that every country will have to revise constantly its position with regard to important organizations like NATO, NORAD, etc., so as to always remain in control of a constantly changing situation, especially since the advent of nuclear arms.
Mr. Speaker, considering the Canadian position and the portion of the Canadian budget which goes every year to national defence, I notice that in 1967-68, we spent $1,693,309,501 and in 1968-69, $1,714,954,800.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the huge amounts allocated to the defence of Europe, to the maintenance of Canadian forces in Europe, to the maintenance of the Canadian presence in NATO contribute to the security of Canada. We see there all the paradox of the world we live in: that we must be armed to the teeth in order to live in peace. To be secure, we must threaten. We must be present, in order not to be attacked. We must spend fabulous sums of money while two thirds of the world population are starving and the other third lives in almost scandalous prosperity.
Mr. Speaker, we are hoping for a revision of the Canadian policy with regard to our participation and our armed forces in NATO; however, we would urge the minister to take measures more peaceful than those aimed simply at defence, because they promote the nuclear arms race and increase the danger hanging over the world. Today, the governments rely mainly on the balance of terror which seems to endanger the whole world. For this reason, our policy is to be reviewed.
The minister stated that we had Canadian forces in Europe. We have to think that situation over and, consequently, it would be advisable to have a more limited and mobile land force which could move very quickly and would be posted in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, following the tour of the various NATO bases in Europe, my colleague from Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) has told me several things. He said that his studies and the trip had shown only one thing; that the world is living in a climate of fear and that Canada is

led like a sheep instead of carrying out a participation policy. He pointed out to me that the Canadian policy was that of a puppet, since we are following the policy of other countries without having a truly Canadian one.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take more time, so I conclude by saying that we hope the minister will do his utmost to work towards greater peace instead of terror. He will also have to do his best to reduce the Caandian forces and the national defence budget, so that the real problem, that of poverty in the world and specially in Canada, may be tackled. This is a problem of peace, understanding and close co-operation, and not of menace and escalation of forces and arms.
Mr. Speaker, we wish the minister to give serious consideration to the matter and resort to every possible influence to prompt other countries to reduce their military commitments, to review their policy in order that we can really live in a peaceful world, and that this peace will not carry a price tag of billions of dollars, as is now the case, but that it be rather brought about through sound cooperation and understanding between human beings. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: OUTLINE OF WORK TO BE ACCOMPLISHED BEFORE SUMMER ADJOURNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the leader of the house very wisely did not attempt to assign any blame for the position in which the government and the house now find themselves, and with great self restraint I shall follow his example.
I might say that he and I have some difference of opinion as to what is, and what is not, highly controversial, but this is not the occasion on which to go into that matter. I believe it is highly desirable-and in this I agree with the thinking of the government-to try to get away from the type of droll mummery and hypocritical farce we have experienced in the past, when target dates were set in an attempt to complete the business of the house and when, in those remaining days, legislative proposals were introduced which no legislative body could be expected to complete in the time allotted.
I think it is an excellent idea to fix a date, and let it be a reasonably firm date, advancing proposals for that period which the house could reasonably be expected to deal with. I also think it highly desirable that there should be a suitable interval between the parts of the session; the government should take at least one month and probably more than two months in which to consider its legislative program so that we may make better progress in the next portion than we have in the present one.
We shall co-operate with the government, provided of course that it is accepted we must discharge our responsibility and duty as
Business of the House
Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. We shall attempt to collaborate and see that the proper measures, as the government has indicated, are passed before the date mentioned. We are also prepared to continue the discussions we are holding with the hon. gentleman and other house leaders to work out ways and means by which some extra time may perhaps be arranged in order to achieve this objective.
As the hon. gentleman has pointed out, there now remain eight opposition days which will probably be piled up back to back. I do not think this is a desirable position in which to find ourselves. These are days, of course, which the opposition uses in order to pinpoint what it considers to be proper criticism of the government in its approach to the legislative program and to its. administration of the nation's affairs. I sincerely hope that next session we shall ensure that such a situation is not repeated.
The government will probably be obliged to make a choice as to the measures which will finally be approved. We shall co-operate, as I say, and I hope that given good will on the part of the house between now and the date assigned, the measures which appear reasonably necessary to hon. members will be passed.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: OUTLINE OF WORK TO BE ACCOMPLISHED BEFORE SUMMER ADJOURNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the President of the Privy Council indicated correctly that this is an interim report on discussions which have taken place among the house leaders. I agree with him that even though we have not reached a firm conclusion about whether we can find some extra time, it was a good idea for him to make a statement on the subject in the house today.
With regard to the attempt to set June 27 as a target date for adjournment, I hope I may be permitted to point out that this year the government is in a position to set a target and ask the house to stick to it. This is because of certain changes we have made in the rules. In the past, no government could do this. It used to be that the voting of supply had no cut-off,, and if the house was in an angry mood and declined to grant supply no attempt to adjourn by a fixed date could be successful. But that has been changed, and the new situation places the responsibility on the government, since, as I say, it can set a target date, to decide which pieces of legislation are to be dealt with, and which should be left over for a subsequent session.

June 2, 1969
Business oj the House
There are a number of important items, including several which have been cited to us more than once during the session, which are not now included in the list read to us. For example, there was to have been an Indian claims bill, or legislation generally respecting the position of Indians in Canada. We understand there is to be a policy statement by the Minister for Indian Affairs and Northern Development, but no legislation regarding Indians is now included in the list presented to us. Neither is there anything on the list regarding veterans, neither in connection with the implementation of the Woods report nor by way of amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act. On the various lists we have been given this session an item has appeared headed "Old Age Security Act amendment". I have never been able to find out either publicly or privately what is involved in this amendment, but whatever it is it seems to be down the drain. References were made to the Canada water bill, which is not now on the list, and there have also been references to a federal co-operatives bill, something which has been kicked around for 50 or 60 years. It is still not there.
Then there is the usual talk about the Canada Development Corporation, an idea which has been around for only five or six years; it will probably be around for a lot longer, still. Nothing appears on the list with regard to labour legislation, either implementing proposals contained in the Woods report or the Freedman report, or dealing in any way with unemployment insurance. In other words, there is a long list of legislation which was proposed for this session but which has been put off until next session- and things which are put off until next session have a way of being put off for a long time after that.
Nevertheless, if it is the government's decision that the house must adjourn on a specific date we think it is our duty to co-operate in the time which is available. But if extra time is to be found I would urge that some of it be used to deal with some of the important items which I have listed but which have not been mentioned today by the government house leader.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
I am pleased also that within the context of his remarks the minister referred to the possibility of certain standing committees of the house meeting in September. I urge strongly that this be done, for two reasons. First, certain committees ought to meet to deal with

matters which have been referred to them. If the Woods report is not ready for reference to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs by the end of June, perhaps that report could be ready for such reference by September. Likewise, there are other committees which ought to me,et in September to deal with business referred to them. But I urge this course of action for a second reason. We all know that we have improved our procedures in the House of Commons, but in so doing have put an extra heavy load on our standing committees. Some of us think that we must move ahead to a time when the committees have the opportunity to meet when the house is not in session. For that reason in particular I urge strongly that plans be made, if it is not decided to bring the house back in September, for a number of committees to meet in September. Let us get this practice started.
I am interested in the statement the minister made, which was more or less in these words: "If the Minister of Finance gives notice of tax changes tomorrow, these changes will have to be dealt with during this session." Since we will begin dealing tomorrow with a tax bill which was left over from last year's budget, I wonder what is the government's hurry during the present session in dealing with matters that will be placed before the house tomorrow night. Mind you, if those changes are tax cuts the government will be amazed at how ready the opposition will be to co-operate.
Again, we welcome this interim statement about what is ahead for us. The minister is quite right in saying that consultation is going on. We are looking into ways and means to find additional time. We will take part in these discussions; but we hope the government will pay attention to those priorities which some of us think are important and which vary somewhat from the priorities set by the government.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out at the outset of my brief remarks that the announcement of the president of the Privy Council was made in English only and that
June 2, 1969

we would have greatly appreciated having it in French so that we might be able to understand it better.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I should like to come back to what was said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), namely that the government is complaining about the fact that only 19 sitting days remain, which is a relatively short period, and that we should not sit in July and come back in September.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that under the new Standing Orders, it is not the responsibility of the opposition to set that target date of June 27. The government is setting it; however, we would be prepared to sit past June 27 in order to study legislation relating to eastern agriculture, which is not found at the present time in the current legislative program.
I would point out that a committee on agriculture will meet in Quebec City at the Chateau Frontenac. But this is not the place where the farmers are found; they are in the fields and therefore the report of that committee will not be dealt with by the house.
At the present time the dairy industry in Quebec goes through a stagnation period, the dairy policy is unacceptable and there has been no review of that dairy policy during this session.
Therefore, this committee will go through studies as a face-saving device, but the recommendations it could make will not be submitted to the house. That is the reason why we would like some more or less important measures to be put aside and replaced by a review of the dairy policy.
I would like to make another remark as to item No. 66, respecting the production and conservation of oil and gas.

I believe we could be spared the discussion of that item from now until June 27, for the simple reason that we will have this week the pleasure of greeting more than 24 United States senators and congressmen, who come to meet the Canadian parliamentarians in order to discuss this question and the possibility of coming to agreements.
I cannot see the house making decisions, passing a bill and holding discussions at the same time. We are paying for the trip of parliamentarians-which will be very expensive-in order to discuss those same questions with the United States representatives. I think there is duplication here, that we could

29180-590J

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Transport):
speechtext:
1. It has been the policy for successive Canadian Governments to have year-round navigation on the St. Lawrence River to the extent that it was practical. Winter navigation was negligible until about ten years ago when changing trading conditions, a better understanding of the problems of operating ships in ice, the entry into the area of European ship owners with ice strengthened ships and the development by the Department of improved measures to support shipping in ice encouraged owners and operators to attempt winter sailings. Since then winter navigation into the Gulf and the St. Lawrence to Quebec has increased rapidly and considerably. Above Quebec winter traffic has developed more recently and slowly because the ice conditions make ship movement more difficult and icebreakers must give priority to flood prevention work and their help is less readily available.
Expected cost in 1969-70 of winter operations is: (a) East of Quebec City, $750,500; (b) West of Quebec City, $877,100.
Figures in (a) are only approximate because of the difficulty of separating the costs of Gulf and Lower River ice operations. Some growth in winter traffic can be absorbed without incurring additional costs of icebreakers and other resources.
2.	No. The present system of aids to navigation is adequate for ships navigating under winter conditions in the St. Lawrence River.
3 and 4. Some study of charges to users for the cost of supporting winter navigation has been done by the Department but no satisfactory formula has yet been found and it is not at present Government policy to charge users for ice-breaking or any other government furnished aids to navigation. If charges for icebreaking are instituted, it would be equitable to apply them to the Gulf and all other ice congested areas and not only to the St. Lawrence.

1.	Are Canada Council Awards for study and research paid in a lump sum and, if not, what is the method of payment?
2.	Has the Canada Council the power to withdraw an award to a person who misuses his award

funds by withdrawing from an approved program of study or research to engage in political activities?
3.	Does the Canada Council maintain contact with all award winners to assure against misuse and, if so, how is that surveillance maintained?
4.	Does the Canada Council maintain contact with some recipients of awards to assure against misuse and, if so, who has the power to determine which award winners will be kept under surveillance?

I am informed by the Canada Council as follows: 1. Doctoral, post-doctoral and leave fellowships are normally paid in three instalments, respectively of 40, 30 and 30 per cent of the total amount. Unless other arrangements are made, the first instalment is paid approximately one month prior to the date of beginning of tenure; in the case of doctoral fellowships it is made only after the Council has received proof of the award holder's acceptance in the university or other institution where he plans to carry out his program. The second and third instalments are normally paid on request after an interval of at least four months in each case, upon submission of an interim report by the recipient. Partial fellowships (usually for four to eight months) are normally paid in two equal instalments; awards of less than $1,000 are paid in one lump sum.
2. The Canada Council has the power to withdraw any award which, for any reason, is not being used for the purposes stated by the recipient in his application and approved by the Council at the time of the award.
3 and 4. Before paying the second and third instalments, the Council requires the award-holder to submit a request together with an interim report on his work. Under the conditions of award, the award holder is also required to seek Council approval for any major change in his work program or in the place of tenure. In the case of a doctoral fellowship holder, any proposed change must be supported in writing by the director of his department. Within six months after the end of the period of tenure, all award holders are required to submit a final report on their work. These requirements enable the Council to maintain contact with award holders. Surveillance is exercised not in relation to the award holders' personal or extra-curricular activities, but in relation to the carrying out of his approved program of work. If the Council has any reason to believe that an award holder's activities interfere with his approved program and could bring into question the effective use of his award, the matter
June 2, 1969

is investigated and the Council may withdraw the award if this is warranted.

speakeroldname: Mr. Walter C. Carter (St. John's West):
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 WATER RESOURCES NEWFOUNDLAND-POLLUTION OF PLACENTIA BAY-NATIONAL PARK-BELL ISLAND EMPLOYMENT-AIRPORT FACILITIES-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I request leave under Standing Order 26 to move that this house do now adjourn to discuss a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely the critical economic plight of the people of Newfoundland due to the failure of the responsible ministers to plan and implement remedies for the grievances caused by the phosphorous pollution of Placentia Bay and St. Mary's Bay, with the consequent loss of livelihood of the fishermen of that area as a result of the failure of the federal government to ensure that necessary precautions were taken before the plant commenced operations.
I move this motion in view of the failure of the government to enter into an agreement with Newfoundland for the establishment and development of a national park on Newfoundland's west coast which would substantially reduce the economic disparity of the region, the failure of the government to come to grips with the serious unemployment and social problems on Bell Island since the closing of the mine in 1966, the failure of the federal government to develop essential international airport facilities at Gander, thereby depriving the people of the east coast of Newfoundland from sharing in the advantages accruing from a modern international airport.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 WATER RESOURCES NEWFOUNDLAND-POLLUTION OF PLACENTIA BAY-NATIONAL PARK-BELL ISLAND EMPLOYMENT-AIRPORT FACILITIES-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The hon. member for St. John's West has proposed that the business of the house be set aside for the purpose of discussing a number of problems in the province of Newfoundland. Actually my interpretation of this motion is that it is in the form of a series of grievances.
June 2, 1969

As hon. members know, the provisions of Standing Order 26 are not intended to provide additional opportunities for the purpose of discussing grievances. It seems that no useful purpose could be served by moving the adjournment of the house to consider what are essentially problems of a continuing nature, one of which, according to the hon. member, goes back to 1966.
The Standing Order applies to a sudden emergency where an immediate debate, given priority over the announced business of the house, might influence the course of immediately impending government action of a specific nature. And, according to the rules and precedents, even if there is urgency of debate, adjournment under Standing Order 26 cannot be granted if there are other opportunities for debate within a reasonable time.
On this particular point, hon. members have heard the discussion which took place earlier today on motions. They might come to the conclusion I have reached, that there will be a number of opportunities open to hon. members who may wish to debate the several grievances raised in the hon. member's proposed motion. In particular, as has been mentioned by hon. members during the short debate on the ministerial statement of the President of the Privy Council, the six-day budget debate will begin tomorrow night and should be continued within a reasonable time thereafter.
As we approach the end of the current semester provided by Standing Order 58, the actual number of remaining allotted days becomes increasingly relevant. There are still eight allotted days in the period which will lapse automatically at the end of this month by reason of the operation of Standing Order 58. We therefore have a total of 14 sitting days that can be used for such purposes between now and the end of the month.
In the circumstances, the hon. member's proposed motion cannot be considered at this time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Leo Cadieux (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: NATO-INQUIRY AS TO EXTENT OF REDUCTION PROPOSED AT BRUSSELS MEETING RESPECTING CANADIAN FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am trying to analyse the question posed by the Leader of the Opposition. First of all, he is talking of the precise response to the ministerial guidance I indicated we would be following. If he would care to read the communique I tabled he will find this particular phrase: "In particular the conventional capability, flexibility and mobility".
We are talking here of the forces that should be committed for use in NATO. The proposal I made in the name of the Canadian government was according to this ministerial guidance. Incidentally, this flows from a study made by Canadian officers which in my estimation is a prefiguration of what the forces will be in the future. I cannot be precise on numbers. I think I indicated in a press conference you can either overestimate or underestimate a force of that nature. The proposal that was made could be described as a self-contained force which would be stripped as much as possible of a ponderous administrative organization. I think we can say that what we propose would not reduce the number of bayonets, if we could call it that. It would be a force that would be flexible and would have back of it the howitzers and gun ships. This would be a brand new thing. We believe it would be very worth while and helpful to the situation in Europe.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when you called it four o'clock last Friday, I was saying that the government was not serious in the least and had no intention whatever of truly helping Canadians in the low income bracket to become home owners or even to acquire one day adequate housing which they can afford.
In my opinion, Bill C-192 is not designed to help the Canadian people. The only trust it is meant to help is, I believe, the profiteering trust which, for the last three years, has increased the interest rate on mortgage loans.
The cost of building materials has never been as high as it is today, lots have never been so dear, the interest rate has never been so prohibitive, the direct and indirect tax on building materials has never been so heavy. School and civic taxes on lots and houses have never been so high.
And how does Bill C-192 propose to correct the situation? To extend the reimbursement period for the loans, in some cases up to 40 years! Mr. Speaker, that is to care not at all about the Canadian people, especially about those in need of houses or dwellings. If the government does not try to reduce the interest rate and the price of land so that housing construction might be possible, if it does not reduce the price of building materials, if it does not assist municipalities with their residential development, if it does not abolish the tax on building materials, I submit, Mr. Speaker, that Bill C-192 is nothing but a monstrous "fake" and mere window-dressing to fool those who are not at all conversant with finance. In fact, for those who know something about finance, it is a monumental farce.
If the Canadian people were aware of these facts and of the double play indulged in by politicians who spout high sounding words like "the just society" but who are, in fact the slaves of high finance, I say that in no time at all they would send home those politicians who are unable to give them the results they want.
We members of the Ralliement creditiste intend to continue to expose the injustices of our present society and the submission of people to the whims of high finance.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity
June 2, 1969

to congratulate the minister on his appointment as minister in charge of reporting for the crown corporation, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. At this time I would like to thank the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) for his hard work over the years and his deep concern for the working people of this great nation regarding their housing problems.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
The riding of London East is comprised of part of the old city of London and the new part which was annexed a few years ago. The people in the offices and factories of our great city are hard workers, and they take great pride in the development of their city. Many have bought homes in the new subdivisions and many others are patiently waiting for their turn. This bill, I hope, will fulfil all of their dreams.
I consider Bill C-192 to be one of the most important pieces of legislation that has come before this new parliament. This bill reaches the very heart of many problems facing the people of this nation. Every Canadian family should be entitled to a home, if they desire one, as a basic, human right. We have been told that the average wage earners in the $5,000 to $7,500 range, who in most cases do not qualify for public housing assistance, should not have to seek such assistance in any case. With the present general level of living costs and with single family dwelling prices what they are, the home ownership dream of many of our Canadian families is just that-a dream.
I ask all hon. members to look at these figures of $5,000 to $7,500. They work out to an average weekly wage of a little over $96 up to over $144. How many working Canadians make these wages? Approximately 1,663,120 people do. What happened to the old concept of some years ago according to which we were told that the guideline should be one week's wage for one month's rent or one month's mortgage payment? That was all the home seeker could afford without going into debt. The only time this theory works is when one applies for a mortgage and is told, "But you do not make enough money." Mr. Speaker, there is something wrong with our system when the average Canadian cannot afford to buy a home that eventually he can call his own. Somebody is making a lot of money, and it is certainly not the average Canadian.
National Housing Act
In view of the desire of most people to own their own homes, and also in view of the high cost of housing, it is clear that there is no one solution to the housing problem. Since the cost of housing is affected by many factors such as the cost of land, the cost of material, the cost of labour, and the cost of financing, it would require a substantial reduction in the cost of these factors before a significant solution could be found to our housing problem. Unfortunately, a close analysis of these facts soon reveals that little can be done to reduce costs. A reduction of approximately $5,000 would be required before the average wage earner could begin to consider buying a home.
It is obvious that some measures can be taken to account for a small portion of this sum. For example, an end to land speculation might account for perhaps $1,000, depending on the area and the availability of land. Reducing the interest rate might result in a large long term saving, but the monthly payment would be reduced only slightly. However, a lower interest rate would affect very little the selling price of the house or the down payment on it. On the other hand, a lower interest rate might reduce moneys available for housing. The cost of materials could also be reduced by the reduction or removal of the taxes imposed upon materials, but the government must then find other means of raising revenue lost by such action. In analysing the last factor in the high cost of housing, the cost of labour, one need only look at the trend in the construction industry to see that a reduction in the cost of labour is impossible. If the steps I have outlined are taken, the reduction in the cost of housing would still not approach the $5,000 figure required. Therefore some other method is required to reduce the costs further.
One method would be low cost housing, the use of new techniques to reduce the amount of outside labour required, as well as the reduction, where possible, of the amount of material required, and the replacement of some costly materials with less expensive but otherwise adequate types. This method, however, is not permitted in some areas because of building codes which are outdated and pertain to antiquated construction methods.
A complete revision of the national building code with an eye to the future would help to reduce the cost of housing, especially in respect of floor area requirements. The national building code of Canada, in my opinion, is the only existing code which has any

June 2, 1969
National Housing Act
chance of universal acceptance. It should be constantly updated and applied from east to west across this great land of ours, with no exceptions. The manufacturers of building materials could then achieve the lowest possible cost, because their production runs could be put on a year-round basis and common articles could be mass produced. Designers of buildings waste many man hours redesigning structures to suit the requirements of the individual communities in which they are built. The designer must spend hours studying in detail the building regulations of each community in order to be sure that his building will conform to local requirements. A standard national building code would eliminate these wasted man hours.
The processing of raw acreage lands into registered building lots, with paved roads and sidewalks, is an important part of house construction. This phase of construction is one of the most troublesome problems for house builders. Speculation, delay due to red tape, and excessive demands for subdivision services have all added to the increase in the cost of building lots and have slowed the development of houses in many areas. Municipalities should extend services quickly enough to put into use a number of serviced lots in excess of demand. They should speed up new zoning laws, and enter into agreements with honest land developers in order to hasten the drawing up of new plans for subdivisions. The availability of plenty of serviced land would bring about a reduction in basic land costs of between $500 to $2,000 per lot, depending on the area.
At this time, Mr. Speaker, I think we should take off our hats to the residential construction industry as it exists in Canada today because construction costs have risen less than the cost of most other commodities. Only an efficient industry could have done that. Most builders now make extensive use of many articles that are precut, prepainted and finished in a factory before they are delivered to the job.
In the ridings of London East, London West and Middlesex, there are hundreds of acres of raw land. If the three levels of government moved together and eliminated the red tape and excessive land profiteering, and if private enterprise were permitted to construct housing through programs unhindered by lack of serviced land, we could soon put all our people into homes they could afford.
People should be allowed to choose whether they wish to live in high-rise apartments or

homes with small lots at rentals or mortgage payments equal to the wage they earn. We should have new subdivisions with new homes for people to move into before we allow older homes to be torn down in any building renewal scheme. If it is feasible to renovate the older homes, then the provinces or cities should take it upon themselves to do this.
The new housing legislation introduced by this government will go a long way toward helping to cure our housing problems if all levels of government, together with the building industry and labour, co-operate in the interests of all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT. 1954 AMENDMENTS CLARIFYING DEFINITIONS AND DEALING WITH THE INTEREST RATE ON INSURED LOANS, AND OTHER MATTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, other members of the official opposition have dealt with various aspects of the proposed amendments to the National Housing Act and of the speech made by the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras) in charge of housing. Today I just want to emphasize two or three points, and I hope I will not be too long.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
First of all, I would like to say to the minister that by removing the freeze on public housing projects and by redirecting a greater part of the C.M.H.C. budget toward low income housing, I think he is demonstrating a sincere concern for the housing needs of Canadians with low incomes. I think he has also demonstrated his view that the freeze was probably a mistake in the first place. I compliment him on taking this step. We in our party support him in this action and we encourage him to do much more in this regard. Three-quarters of the wage-earners of this country have incomes of less than $5,000 a year. I understand that as many Canadian workers earn less than $4,000 as make more than that amount. Canadians with small incomes have two separate types of housing problems. The first, of course, is bad housing, often made worse by overcrowding. This accommodation ranges from places where the roof is falling in to places where there is no plumbing. Housing of this type is still a serious and widespread concern.
The second problem is, of course, that of high rents and prices. Housing experts agree that a family should not spend more than 20 per cent of its income on shelter. For a family which earns $3,000 a year this means $50 a month. Even if it is held that a family may spend 25 per cent of its income on shelter it amounts to something like $60 a month. But
June 2, 1969

very few Canadians can find any housing or, at least, good housing, at this price. The result is, of course, that many thousands of Canadians living on low incomes pay a much higher proportion of those incomes for housing than is proper.
Each of these problems is bad enough in itself, but the two are often combined-bad housing and high prices. In human terms, the price is one which Canada cannot afford. This is why the modest effort presented to the house by the minister will receive our support and why we insist that much more must be done.
The proposed amendment to section 35C will be useful in connection with the land assembly program as well as for public housing and residential development. It is all to the good. I notice that the minister, in order to get the loans for this land assembly program going, is consulting with the provinces-at least, that is my understanding. I say this is right. It should have been done at the outset when the task force began its operations. I emphasize the need for speedy action. Programs involving land assembly take time before becoming effective and this one should have been under way long since. It should have been in high gear by this time.
As the operation of supply and demand continues, land prices continue to spiral. The results are all too clear for us to see. While over-all housing costs rose by 80 per cent between 1961 and 1968, the price of serviced land increased by 240 per cent. This is why we in our party have for some time placed emphasis on the need for the federal government to involve itself in a land bank program even though many supporters of the party opposite described this during the election campaign as socialism. I must stress how far short the minister's program falls of what is required in connection with housing in Canada today. I want, for the good of the country, indeed for the sake of the very unity of the country, to force this government to understand that the need for housing is in many cases critical and desperate and to come to terms with the long range underlying economic factors which have produced this crisis in housing affecting Canadians with low incomes.
Housing cannot be considered in isolation. It must be considered in relation to broader economic programs. Obviously, inflation has a great bearing on the difficulties which many experience in connection with housing. Continued inflation imposes a particularly serious 29180-591
National Housing Act
burden on Canadians receiving lower incomes. I must once again describe the efforts of this government to combat inflation as halfhearted and ineffective. There is no need for me to elaborate. It is sufficient to say that the only program so far adopted by the government to fight inflation has been the establishment of a prices and incomes commission recommended, after many months of delay, in December. The chairman of this commission was appointed only this month and as far as we know the balance of the commission has yet to be appointed.
An adequate housing program must be integrated with an effective anti-poverty program. The Economic Council has documented the incidence of poverty in Canada. Yet the government abandoned the war against poverty even before it was begun; any machinery which had been set up to co-ordinate an effective approach was dismantled despite the fact the Economic Council had called on the government of Canada to accept the challenge of poverty in the nation and to meet with the provinces for the purpose of mapping out an integrated attack. As far as we can see, nothing has been done in this regard.
Then, of course, in addition to general economic programs, the control of inflation and an effective integrated anti-poverty program, policies related to environment are obviously essential in carrying out a housing program on any scale. The minister talks about pollution but little action is taken, and I am sure there is no effective organization within the government to develop, let alone carry out, effective, co-ordinated programs or to provide leadership in this country in the battle against pollution. Indeed, if one looks at the over-all housing policy, if one considers the attitude of the government toward inflation, if one considers the lack of any organized attack upon poverty, one is impressed only by the chaos which exists in government planning. In fact, I would say that the chaos in this field is almost as bad as the chaos which has developed in the area of national defence.
The proposals of the government as put forward by the minister are halfhearted. Why was it necessary for the people of Canada to wait a whole year for this little program which is now being proposed? Why should the people looking for housing, the people experiencing housing difficulties, have to wait a whole year for the government to come forward with these inadequate proposals? I suggest part of the reason is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has a constitutional hang-up. And part of the reason is that he

June 2, 1969
National Housing Act
does not believe that housing represents much of a problem for Canadians.
I have a good deal of sympathy for the position taken by the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) when he said last week: "I cannot understand for the life of me how we got into a constitutional question with regard to housing." The hon. member's real difficulty lies in understanding the Prime Minister, and I do not blame him for that. One day the Prime Minister says that under the constitution as it stands we are unable to attack problems of housing and pollution on any level of government. Speaking in the House of Commons on February 14 last the Prime Minister, in referring to the challenge of pollution and difficulties in the area of housing said, as reported at page 5524 of Hansard:
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
This challenge of pollution of our rivers and lakes, of our farmlands and forests and of the very air we breathe, cannot be met effectively in our federal state without some constitutional reform or clarification. It is important that we know which level of government is responsible and, if both, In what way they are ready to co-operate through the use of the spending power and other devices to permit these problems to be tackled properly.
I believe this is true of many other problems which are sometimes brought to the attention of this house, problems such as urban renewal of housing and urban transport. These problems cannot be dealt with properly because the present constitution is either silent or vague about the level of government which has the legal competence to tackle them. Until the constitution is brought into the 20th century in some of these respects, governments are to a large degree powerless to solve the problems either by acting alone or in co-operation with other levels of government.
On February 14, therefore, the Prime Minister expressed a viewpoint about certain constitutional difficulties. The former minister of transport believed that the Prime Minister held those views. On the one hand, the Prime Minister said that under our present constitution no level of government, alone or in cooperation with other levels, can do an adequate job with housing and urban problems. On the other hand, on the day the former minister of transport resigned his portfolio the Prime Minister said:
But the history of these facts will demonstrate that we took this position from the start, that most of the fundamental issues in this country could be settled under the present constitution through co-operation between the federal government and the provinces.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is it possible to take seriously a Prime Minister who says in February that certain problems cannot be resolved until there is a constitutional change

and who says immediately after a minister resigns that, after all, these problems can be solved under the present constitution through co-operation? I ask the real Prime Minister of this country to stand up. It is difficult for us to know which of these views he holds.
The Prime Minister may have important views affecting our ability to solve certain problems under the existing constitution. Nevertheless I must say emphatically that we cannot wait for constitutional reforms before making a serious attack on housing and other problems. Having read his remarks I have concluded that fundamentally the Prime Minister does not believe the solution of this problem is important. Neither does he believe that the problem of housing is urgent in Canada. As a result the government has dragged its feet for the past year and used constitutional difficulties as an excuse.
When the former deputy prime minister of this country who was in charge of housing resigned, what happened? There was a little flurry of activity which led to no effective organization of planning procedures. There has been no effective move to co-ordinate and develop housing programs and relate those programs to other valid programs dealing with poverty in Canada. Therefore the program the minister has introduced appears to be simply a reaction to his predecessor's resignation.
I say emphatically to my colleagues in the house that it is our duty to keep the heat on the minister and the government. The government not only must move forward with the type of housing program we need but it must also establish machinery that will deal with other programs related to the areas of pollution, poverty or what have you. It must establish effective programs that will deal with housing needs and with other related needs of the people. Unless heat is applied to the minister and the government the fear brought on by the resignation of the former deputy prime minister will quickly evaporate.
Our problems must be attacked effectively. We have suggested that planning ought to be brought under the authority of a department of housing and urban affairs which would coordinate research and planning and give leadership in developing policy in this field. Someone may have a better idea than this. The government may have something better in mind. If so, it ought to bring it forward. Certainly, sir, giving limited responsibility to a Minister without Portfolio, earnest though he may be, just will not do. Certainly any
June 2, 1969



authority C.M.H.C. may have will not prove adequate for the job that is to be done.
As I say, we are at present considering the government's reaction to a fright resulting from the resignation of a minister. We are not dealing seriously with a co-ordinated attack on housing problems and other related problems in this country. When one considers how little is being done in this measure to help low income Canadians obtain decent homes, one can come to no other conclusion. Certainly something is being done about public housing, but what do the minister's proposals mean for the hundreds of thousands of Canadian families not eligible for low income housing? Those families have incomes of not more than $8000 or $9000 a year. They must earn more if they are to afford a home financed under the provisions of the National Housing Act. I ask, in what way do the minister's proposals assist those hundreds of thousands of Canadians? For those people this measure surely is a mockery.
